Sliding window is a technique for a running range over a sequence, kept as two indices, left and right, that only move forward, plus a running summary of what sits between them: a sum, a count of distinct values, a table of occurrences. Instead of recomputing that summary for every range considered, you update it as one element enters at the right and, when the range needs to shrink, another leaves at the left.

The shape of problem that signals it is a question about a contiguous run, a substring or a subarray rather than any subset, asking for the longest, the shortest, the maximum or a count, where the property you watch stays true as the run gets shorter. "Longest substring with no repeated character", "shortest subarray whose sum reaches a target" and "longest run of ones after k flips" are this shape. A question about a subsequence, where elements need not sit next to each other, is not: no window applies to it.

The mechanism is the window invariant, the property the range must hold at the moment you read off the answer. For a longest window, the new element goes in first, then you shrink from the left in a loop, not an

, until the invariant holds again, and only then compare against the best answer. For a shortest window, the order flips: while the invariant already holds, you record the length and try to do without the leftmost element. Because left only ever moves forward and never further than right, the whole pass across n elements does O(n) work, even with a loop inside the loop.
The mistake that shows up under pressure is shrinking with an

, which removes one element and stops even when the range is still invalid, so the answer quietly comes from a broken window. The other is a sum-based invariant on data that can be negative: removing an element from the left can then raise the sum, so the shrink loop stops in the wrong place and the answer is wrong with no error at all.

You meet this in the interview question itself: find the largest sum of any k consecutive readings, or, in the harder variable form, the longest run satisfying some running condition, both solved in one pass with nothing more than a running total or a small table beside the two indices.

is the property the window has at the point where you read the answer. For "longest run with at most two distinct values" it is "the window holds at most two distinct values". The entering element is the only thing that can break it, and the inner loop exists to restore it. When you explain a solution, state the invariant first: the code, the loop condition and the place where the answer is read all follow from it.

Shrinking can restore the invariant only when the property is monotone. A window with at most two distinct values still has at most two after you remove an element, and a window with three still has three after you add one. A sum behaves like that only when no element is negative. With a negative element, removing an element from the left can raise the sum, and the loop stops in the wrong place. The last section of this topic shows the counterexample, and the fix comes with prefix sums.
The nested loop is O(n) in total, not O(n²).

It is the same argument as for amortised vector growth in the complexity topic: one step can cost O(n), but all the steps together cost O(n). The extra space is whatever the summary needs: O(1) for a sum, and O(size of the alphabet) or O(k) for a table of counts.
